readings.title: The Library of Useful Things
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
At the North Gate Library, a shelf of power drills once attracted more questions than the latest novels. The library had started lending simple tools after staff noticed that many residents needed a device for one small repair but did not want to buy it. The first month was awkward. A borrower returned a drill without its charger, and several others asked librarians for technical advice they were not trained to give.

Director Mei Chen invited local repairers to redesign the service. They attached a picture checklist to each case so borrowers and staff could count the parts together. A volunteer recorded short demonstrations, but the videos explained safe handling and basic controls only; they did not promise that every home repair would be easy. When a task seemed risky, the catalogue advised people to seek a qualified worker.

The library also changed how it measured success. At first, staff counted loans. Yet a popular tool might sit unused in someone's cupboard for a week. Now borrowers may attend a monthly practice evening before taking a tool home. They can try it on scrap wood and ask questions. The evening has led to fewer missing parts, but its greater value may be the confidence of people who once thought a repair was beyond them.

Not everyone wants to borrow a drill. Some visitors use the library's sewing machine, while others come only to hear how a neighbour fixed a loose chair. Mei insists that ordinary books still matter. The new service simply extends the library's old purpose: making knowledge and useful resources available to more people. She hopes other libraries will copy the idea, but only after listening to what their own neighbourhoods actually need.

options.B: Residents sometimes needed a device for a brief task.

options.D: Repairers wanted to advertise new equipment.

readings.title: A Path for More People
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
The city of Bellhaven advertised its new hilltop garden as "open to everyone." Yet its only entrance was a long staircase. On opening day, guide Luis noticed two visitors studying the sign at the bottom before turning away. One used a walking frame; the other pushed a child in a stroller. Luis reported what he had seen, and the parks office invited residents to describe their journeys to the garden.

The first proposal was a straight paved ramp up the hill. It looked efficient on a drawing, but its slope would have been tiring and difficult to use safely. A landscape architect suggested a longer path that followed the natural curve of the ground. It reached the same viewpoint more gradually, passed several shaded places to rest, and avoided removing an old oak tree. Some council members objected that a longer route would cost more to maintain.

To learn how the path might work, the team marked a temporary route with small flags. Residents walked it at different times of day. A wheelchair user found that a narrow turn left too little room to change direction. A parent said the shade was welcome, but the surface became slippery after rain. These comments changed the final plan: the turn was widened, the surface was redesigned, and signs gave the distance to the next resting place.

When the garden reopened, Luis noticed visitors who had never reached the top before. He also saw runners choose the new route because they liked the trees. The path had not made every part of the hill equally accessible; a steep side trail remained unsuitable for many people. The parks office described that limit clearly on its map. Luis thought the honesty mattered. A promise of access should help people plan a visit, not merely look attractive on a poster.

readings.title: Skills Across the Table
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
At a community centre in Larch Street, a retired electrician named Omar wanted to learn how to make video calls. Across the room, university student Priya needed help repairing a desk lamp. A notice board called the programme a "skill exchange," but neither person thought of their knowledge as valuable enough to offer. Omar assumed every young person could use any digital service. Priya assumed electrical work required tools she could never understand.

The coordinator paired them for a one-hour meeting, with two rules. Each person would name one small goal, and neither would touch the other's device without permission. Priya showed Omar how to join a call, then asked him to repeat the steps while she watched. He wrote down the sequence in words that made sense to him. Later, Omar inspected the lamp with Priya. When he saw a damaged cable, he stopped. He explained that replacing it required a qualified professional and showed her how to recognise the warning signs instead.

The meeting did not produce a working lamp, yet Priya left satisfied. She had learned when a repair was beyond a beginner, a skill as useful as tightening a screw. Omar made his first video call to a cousin that evening. At the next session, he returned with a question about adjusting the volume. Priya arrived with a new goal: learning to read a simple electricity bill.

Over six months, the centre found that the strongest partnerships changed partners' assumptions as much as their practical abilities. People who were used to teaching had to practise asking questions; people who usually received help discovered things they could explain. The coordinator still matched participants carefully and did not pretend that an hour of conversation could replace professional training. But a small, equal exchange could make learning less lonely and more precise.

readings.title: The Day Trip That Stayed Local
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A travel club in Millford used to advertise its weekend trips with photographs of crowded landmarks. Members spent hours on a coach, hurried through a famous market, and returned with little memory of the people who worked there. When the club asked for fresh ideas, member Elsa suggested visiting the town of Fenwick, only forty minutes away by train. Several members doubted that such a nearby place could feel like a holiday.

Elsa met Fenwick's tourism officer before planning the trip. The officer explained that a family-run bakery welcomed small groups in the morning, but its busiest hours were unsuitable for tours. A local history volunteer could lead a walk after lunch. Elsa arranged a group of twelve, paid the volunteer for the preparation as well as the walk, and gave travellers a choice between buying lunch from local shops or bringing their own. No shop was promised customers it might not receive.

On the day, the group travelled by train and walked between stops. At the bakery, the owner described how flour prices affected her menu. She answered questions while the ovens were cooling, and the visitors bought what they wanted without pressure. In the afternoon, the volunteer showed them a flood marker hidden behind a modern bridge. Its height led to a conversation about how the town had changed its building rules.

The trip was less polished than the club's old tours: rain shortened the final walk, and one cafe had no seats left. Yet members said they understood more about Fenwick than they had expected. Elsa's report did not claim that a short train ride alone made the visit responsible. The important choices were to respect working schedules, pay for local knowledge, keep the group manageable, and allow residents to say no. A nearby destination had given the club room to travel more thoughtfully.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese.

A public space becomes useful when people can understand how to enter and take part. A sign that says "all welcome" is a good beginning, but it cannot remove every obstacle. Visitors may need clear directions, a place to rest, or permission to join an activity quietly before speaking. Organizers can ask people about these needs and test their plans in real conditions. They should also explain honestly what a service cannot provide. Such small choices show respect for different ways of moving, learning, and spending time. When people feel able to choose their own level of participation, a library, park, or community centre can become a place to which they want to return.
translation.explanation: 仅供自评。注意all welcome的语境含义，what a service cannot provide的宾语从句，以及to which引导的定语从句；按意义、准确性和中文表达评分。
translation.referenceAnswer: 当人们知道如何进入并参与时，公共空间才能真正发挥作用。“欢迎所有人”的标语是一个良好的开端，却不能消除所有障碍。来访者可能需要清晰的指引、休息的地方，或是在开口发言前先安静参与活动的自由。组织者可以向人们询问这些需求，并在真实条件下检验方案。他们也应坦诚说明某项服务无法提供什么。这些细小的选择体现了对不同出行方式、学习方式和休闲方式的尊重。当人们觉得可以自行选择参与程度时，图书馆、公园或社区中心就能成为他们愿意再来的地方。

criteria.name: 意义完整
criteria.description: 完整传达公共空间的可参与性、具体障碍、试行方案与诚实说明等主要信息。

criteria.name: 语言准确
criteria.description: 准确处理条件、并列、宾语从句和定语从句，无重大误译。

criteria.name: 表达自然
criteria.description: 中文通顺，句间衔接清楚，符合书面表达习惯。

writing.stem:
Write at least 100 words in English on the following topic: A Better First Visit to a Public Place.

A new community facility near you wants suggestions for helping first-time visitors feel comfortable. Write a short proposal. Describe one difficulty a new visitor might face, suggest two practical improvements, and explain how the staff could learn whether those improvements work. Give an example from a library, park, community centre, or another public place. Do not include your real name or contact details.
writing.explanation: 仅供自评。范文以社区图书馆为例，说明首次到访者可能不知从何开始，提出导览卡和志愿者引导两项措施，并说明如何收集反馈。按任务完成、结构连贯和语言运用评分。
writing.sampleAnswer:
I suggest improving the first visit to our community library. A new visitor may see many rooms and services but still be unsure where to begin. This uncertainty can be especially uncomfortable for someone who does not want to interrupt busy staff.

First, the library could offer a simple card at the entrance. It should show the main rooms, opening hours, and where to ask for help. Second, a volunteer could give an optional five-minute tour. Visitors who prefer to explore alone could decline without explanation.

To find out whether these changes work, staff could ask new visitors one short question as they leave: “Was anything difficult to find?” They could also record which questions are asked most often at the desk. If the same problem continues, the card or tour should be changed. A welcoming place improves by listening to the people who use it.

criteria.name: 任务完成
criteria.description: 交代一个首次到访难点、两项可实施改进及评估办法，内容切题具体。

criteria.name: 组织连贯
criteria.description: 建议书结构清楚，段落和连接自然，论述有条理。

criteria.name: 语言运用
criteria.description: 词汇和语法基本准确，句式有变化，达到至少100词。
